channel.title: OSA Paper Podcast
channel.description:
Every day, one new paper on obstructive sleep apnea surgery: hypoglossal nerve stimulation, palate surgery including barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, tongue base, skeletal and nasal procedures, patient selection and comparators. Every episode summarizes the paper, walks through it as a teaching round, places it against a 440-paper evidence library, and ends with whether it should change practice.
Episodes are written and narrated by an AI system working from the full text of each paper and the host's curated library of digests, under rules set by the host. They are reviewed for teaching, not for patient care. Nothing here is medical advice.
Episode guide and subscribe links: https://www.sleepapneaimplant.org/podcast
Produced by Ryan Nord, MD (VCU Health). Disclosures: consultant to AvivoMed; previously a consultant to Inspire Medical Systems (ended 2025) and Medtronic. No company funds or reviews this podcast.

item.title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
item.itunes:title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
item.description:
The take-home point: pain about three out of ten on day one and near zero by one month is a promising early-recovery signal. But it describes one technique, in thirty selected patients, under one fixed protocol.
The first decision it touches is technique choice. In Dr. Nord's practice, B-R-P remains the palate operation of choice. This paper offers an appealing muscle-sparing idea, but no head-to-head data. The evidence that would move that decision is a direct comparison with B-R-P under identical steroids and analgesia. It would need blinded pain scoring, visits through the first two weeks, and sleep testing well beyond six months.
The second decision is counseling. The paper adds a carefully measured early recovery curve. Those numbers belong to the stayed bridge technique, so they should be quoted only as stayed bridge data. For a patient having B-R-P, the counseling numbers still come from the B-R-P series. About one in five have transient swallowing difficulty that settles within a week. Thread extrusion happens in about one in eight across barbed techniques. This paper adds one useful line: sparing the muscle did not make extrusion go away.
The third decision is observation. These patients stayed two days by protocol. In Dr. Nord's practice, airway-surgery patients like these are kept for twenty-three-hour observation. The twelve-hour scores fall inside that window. The twenty-four- and forty-eight-hour scores come after it. The paper did not monitor breathing on the first night, so it can't inform how long that observation should be.
Finally, the Inspire conversation. Dr. Nord is a high-volume Inspire implanter. Patients with this profile, moderate disease, a body mass index under thirty and tonsils present, are the group where Inspire and palate surgery are both on the table. This paper is palate-surgery data. It gives no outcomes by collapse pattern and no post-operative DISE. It adds recovery information on the palate side of that discussion, not Inspire evidence.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Pace A, Iannella G, Maniaci A, Cocuzza S, Moffa A, Alunni Fegatelli D, et al. Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP). *JCM*. 2025;14(20):7402. doi:10.3390/jcm14207402 https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm14207402

item.title: Hypoxic Burden Reduction After Lateral Pharyngoplasty in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Beyond the Apnea-Hypopnea Index
item.itunes:title: Hypoxic Burden Reduction After Lateral Pharyngoplasty in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Beyond the Apnea-Hypopnea Index
item.description:
The take-home point: this paper doesn't alter who is offered palate surgery or Inspire. What it adds is a fuller way to describe results and to counsel patients afterward.
Keep the headline in mind. Whole-night hypoxic burden fell to about a third of baseline. The median went from ninety-seven point one to thirty-five percent-minutes per hour.
The decision it touches is how to read a sleep study labeled a Sher failure. An AHI-only label may undersell what happened to the patient's oxygen. So after palate surgery, it's reasonable to look at hypoxic burden alongside the AHI. If you do, use the same software and scoring rules before and after, or the comparison means little. And be honest with the patient. In this paper, some failures got worse, and supine burden did not significantly improve in that group.
Dr. Nord's practice performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, which is a different operation. Lateral pharyngoplasty cuts the superior constrictor and uses no barbed suture. These numbers shouldn't be carried over to BRP. The literature has no hypoxic burden data for BRP yet.
Dr. Nord's practice is also a high-volume Inspire practice. Dr. Nord has previously consulted for Inspire. For Inspire counseling, the burden data come from the first-generation STAR device and from Inspire IV, not from this palate series. There are no published outcomes yet for Inspire V.
On weight, this paper's signal is small. Successes had a lower body mass index, but in only eight patients per group. In Dr. Nord's practice, weight loss is part of multimodal treatment of obstructive sleep apnea alongside Inspire, often both rather than either-or. That includes glucagon-like peptide one drugs. Many Inspire patients are already on these drugs or will become candidates for them.
Confidence is moderate that burden falls after this operation in selected patients. It is low that Sher failures meaningfully benefit. Four things would move it. A controlled study. Hypoxic burden data after BRP. An analysis showing burden adds information beyond the AHI. And symptom or cardiovascular outcomes.
For the residents: when you present a postoperative sleep study in clinic, bring the oxygen picture along with the AHI.
That was de Aquino's group in Campinas, writing in Sleep and Breathing in 2026.
What's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Vieira ALP, Duarte BB, Almeida AR, Greters ME, Leandro-Merhi VA, de Aquino JLB. "Hypoxic burden reduction after lateral pharyngoplasty in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: Beyond the apnea-hypopnea index." *Sleep and Breathing* (2026) 30:267. DOI: 10.1007/s11325-026-03808-7. PMID: not printed in PDF (42771120 per the weekly PubMed scan). Received 25 May 2026; revised 6 September 2026; accepted 14 September 2026. Open access (CC BY 4.0). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11325-026-03808-7

item.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
item.itunes:title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
item.description:
The call is no change.
The decision this paper touches is the counseling conversation with a patient who carries excess weight and is considering Inspire or barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, BRP. Should a weight-loss medication come first? This paper can't answer that. It has no surgical arm, no implanted patients, no drug-induced sleep endoscopy, and no palate data.
What it does sharpen is the language. Quote drug-specific numbers. With tirzepatide, about twenty-two fewer events per hour than control over a year. With liraglutide, about six fewer than control. Don't quote the pooled ten. Don't promise better oxygenation or a cardiovascular benefit. Don't call these drugs a substitute for CPAP; the authors don't either. And if a patient loses substantial weight before surgery, get a new sleep study before deciding anything.
One more point for residents. Dr. Nord's practice keeps airway-surgery patients like these for twenty-three-hour observation. This paper says nothing about how these drugs affect that perioperative course, so don't cite it for that.
Confidence in no change is fairly high, because the paper restates existing trials rather than adding new ones. What would move it? A randomized trial of a GLP-1 drug before Inspire or BRP, measuring candidacy and surgical response. Data beyond fifty-two weeks, including what happens after stopping. And repeat drug-induced sleep endoscopy after weight loss, to see whether the collapse pattern changes.
Again, that's Aljazeeri's group, "GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials." Sleep and Breathing, 2026, volume thirty, article two seventy-nine.
Residents, before I see you in the operating room or clinic: what's your one takeaway from this paper?
Paper: Carvalhal G, Mora MMR, Peralta-Jiménez GA, Ayasa L, Barrera V, Advani K, et al. GLP-1 receptor agonists for obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. *Sleep Breath*. 2026. doi:10.1007/s11325-026-03826-5 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11325-026-03826-5

item.title: Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes
item.itunes:title: Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes
item.description:
The call for Dr. Nord's practice is no change, with a watch on ultrasound as a research tool.
The decision this paper touches is what to make of tongue motion after implantation. Three pieces.
First, counseling. I won't tell a patient that a strong forward tongue at activation predicts a great sleep study, or that a modest one predicts failure. This paper gives no basis for either, and the Emory data say the same.
Second, titration. There's no support here for using visible or ultrasound motion as a titration target, or for raising amplitude just to make the tongue move more. Motion wasn't related to voltage in their standard-configuration patients. The authors caution against increasing stimulation beyond comfort. That's sensible, but it's their recommendation, not something this study measured.
Third, the non-responder whose tongue moves well. This paper and the Penn work both point away from making the tongue move more, and toward the airway itself. In Dr. Nord's practice, once awake endoscopy and reprogramming have failed, DISE is a good tool for the Inspire non-responder, because it shows the lumen that ultrasound can't. The authors suggest residual palatal or lateral-wall obstruction as one explanation, a hypothesis they didn't test. That's where palate surgery, including barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, enters the discussion, but this paper isn't evidence for it.
What doesn't change? This study says nothing about retraction, or about which nerve branches the cuff captures at implantation. That question still rests on Steffen's group's small series. When I teach residents in the operating room, the point is narrower now: how far the tongue moves forward is not a demonstrated predictor of the sleep study.
Confidence: moderate that graded ultrasound magnitude and symmetry aren't useful predictors at this level of measurement. Low on buckling, where the interval is wide. What would move me is a prospective study with measured displacement, several amplitudes per patient, paired DISE, one standardized full-night study, and adjustment for baseline severity.
The citation: Tschopp, Janjic, Caversaccio, Borner and Tschopp. "Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes." Laryngoscope Investigative Otolaryngology, twenty twenty-six. Volume eleven, issue two.
Residents, what's your one takeaway?
Paper: Tschopp S, Janjic V, Caversaccio M, Borner U, Tschopp K. Ultrasonographic Tongue Base Motion Does Not Correlate With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Outcomes. *Laryngoscope Investig Oto*. 2026;11(2). doi:10.1002/lio2.70376 https://doi.org/10.1002/lio2.70376

item.title: Post-Operative Radiological Evaluation of a Bilateral Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation System
item.itunes:title: Post-Operative Radiological Evaluation of a Bilateral Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation System
item.description:
My call is no change, with one thing to watch.
I'm a high-volume Inspire implanter, and I perform barbed reposition pharyngoplasty. This paper touches neither. It's Genio data from eleven patients. It has nothing on Inspire candidacy, drug-induced sleep endoscopy, or palate surgery, and I won't quote its numbers to an Inspire patient.
The decisions it affects are narrower. When a patient asks about the bilateral device, my counseling stays where Patel and Heiser leave it: there is no demonstrated efficacy advantage over unilateral stimulation, and the safety record is less mature. DREAM adds device-specific failure modes, including migration. When a patient with a Genio implant needs imaging of the floor of mouth or tongue base, I now know what to expect. Plain films show the hardware cleanly. CT will carry artifact, compounded by dental work, and the authors advise reformatting in at least two planes. This is an older population where head and neck cancer workup will come up, as the authors point out, so it's worth telling the radiologist up front.
What I teach residents in the operating room and clinic is this. A symmetric film is not a prediction of success, and an asymmetric one is not grounds for revision. The trigger for workup is failure to activate or failure to respond, not the picture.
My confidence is high that this doesn't touch Inspire practice. It's moderate on the imaging advice, because that rests on eight CT scans in patients who all had dental implants. What would move me? A larger bilateral series with day-one and activation-visit films, linked to thresholds and twelve-month A-H-I. If a day-one film predicted migration or activation failure, that baseline would become actionable. That's the watch.
The citation: Kilgue, Gehl, Abolmaali, Scholtz, Scherl and Todt. Post-operative radiological evaluation of a bilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation system. Frontiers in Surgery, 2026, volume 13, article 1818247.
Residents, what's your one takeaway?

My call is no change, with one thing to watch.

I'm a high-volume Inspire implanter, and I perform barbed reposition pharyngoplasty. This paper touches neither. It's Genio data from eleven patients. It has nothing on Inspire candidacy, drug-induced sleep endoscopy, or palate surgery, and I won't quote its numbers to an Inspire patient.

The decisions it affects are narrower. When a patient asks about the bilateral device, my counseling stays where Patel and Heiser leave it: there is no demonstrated efficacy advantage over unilateral stimulation, and the safety record is less mature. DREAM adds device-specific failure modes, including migration. When a patient with a Genio implant needs imaging of the floor of mouth or tongue base, I now know what to expect. Plain films show the hardware cleanly. CT will carry artifact, compounded by dental work, and the authors advise reformatting in at least two planes. This is an older population where head and neck cancer workup will come up, as the authors point out, so it's worth telling the radiologist up front.

What I teach residents in the operating room and clinic is this. A symmetric film is not a prediction of success, and an asymmetric one is not grounds for revision. The trigger for workup is failure to activate or failure to respond, not the picture.

My confidence is high that this doesn't touch Inspire practice. It's moderate on the imaging advice, because that rests on eight CT scans in patients who all had dental implants. What would move me? A larger bilateral series with day-one and activation-visit films, linked to thresholds and twelve-month A-H-I. If a day-one film predicted migration or activation failure, that baseline would become actionable. That's the watch.

The citation: Kilgue, Gehl, Abolmaali, Scholtz, Scherl and Todt. Post-operative radiological evaluation of a bilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation system. Frontiers in Surgery, 2026, volume 13, article 1818247.

item.title: Auditory Perceptions Associated With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.itunes:title: Auditory Perceptions Associated With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.description:
My call is change, but a narrow one, limited to counseling and to the questions we ask. There's no change to candidacy, no change to surgical technique, and no bearing on barbed reposition pharyngoplasty or other palate decisions.
The first decision affected is the consent conversation for Inspire. I'll tell candidates what our own series showed: in a survey of seventy patients, about one in six noticed a new sound during stimulation, most often described as buzzing, followed by humming and electrical. Five of those twelve said it had no effect on daily life, sleep or mood. Four described a slight effect and three a moderate one. None described a severe effect, and none of the twelve stopped using the device. I'll also give the caveats: one center, a telephone survey, an unvalidated questionnaire, no hearing tests, and an unknown response rate.
Preexisting tinnitus isn't a reason to exclude a patient, and it isn't grounds for absolute reassurance either. Four against eight is too small to settle it. Record tinnitus and hearing history at consent, because this study had to rely on recall to call a sound new.
The second decision is at activation and titration. Ask directly: do you hear anything when the device turns on? Ask which side they sleep on. When a patient's use is slipping, ask whether noise is part of the reason. That link isn't proven, but without targeted questions this effect is easy to miss.
I would not drop the C1 fibers based on this paper; the mechanism is a hypothesis.
On device generation, this paper doesn't state which Inspire models were included. The proposed mechanism doesn't depend on a sensing lead, and there are no published outcomes yet for Inspire V.
My confidence is low to moderate. What would move it is a multicenter prospective study that reports its response rate and includes audiometry, acoustic recordings, laterality, programming changes and longitudinal follow-up. If device sound turned out to drive nonuse or explantation, it would become a patient selection question, not just a counseling one.
The citation: Belilos, Adibi, Tucker, Saeedi, Calder, Lee, and myself. "Auditory Perceptions Associated With Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea." Laryngoscope Investigative Otolaryngology, twenty twenty-six, volume eleven, article e seven zero five five zero.
Residents, here's my question for you: what one auditory question will you add to your next activation visit, and why that one?

item.title: Exploring the Role of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Optimizing Upper Airway Stimulation Therapy for Non-Responders
item.itunes:title: Exploring the Role of Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy in Optimizing Upper Airway Stimulation Therapy for Non-Responders
item.description:
My call is watch.
The exact decision this paper touches is the implanted patient who tolerates the device, has been through the titration study and awake titration, and is still failing. The question is whether to add a DISE with stimulation on before recommending barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, an oral appliance or another operation. Kant's protocol is a reasonable, well-described option for that patient. The paper cannot show that it works better than another round of awake titration, so I'm not calling it a standard step.
Candidacy doesn't change. The pre-implant DISE did not identify who would fail to couple, and no baseline factor did either.
Counselling gets sharper. At this one hospital, about one implant in four, twenty-nine of one hundred and fourteen, needed this step. Of those twenty-nine, eight became responders. Always quote both denominators: eight of twenty-nine, or eight of the eighteen followed. Never call forty-four percent a rescue rate.
For barbed reposition pharyngoplasty after an implant, set expectations as partial benefit, three of seven. Those are airway-surgery patients, kept for twenty-three-hour observation. Oral appliance or uvulectomy produced no responders, zero of five, though that group is tiny.
And Inspire V? The electrode-configuration logic may carry over, because the stimulation lead remains. That is untested. There are no published outcomes yet for Inspire V.
My confidence is low to moderate. What would move me to change practice is a comparison of DISE-guided management against repeated awake titration in matched non-responders, with every patient accounted for, follow-up to twelve months, and usage hours reported.
The citation: Kant E, Hardeman JA, Stokroos RJ, Copper MP. Exploring the role of drug-induced sleep endoscopy in optimizing upper airway stimulation therapy for non-responders. Sleep and Breathing, 2025, volume twenty-nine, article two eighty-five.
Residents, here's my question. When the tongue moves but the palate doesn't follow, what is your next step, and what number would you quote to the patient? What's your one takeaway?
Paper: Kant E, Hardeman JA, Stokroos RJ, Copper MP. Exploring the role of drug-induced sleep endoscopy in optimizing upper airway stimulation therapy for non-responders. *Sleep Breath*. 2025;29(5). doi:10.1007/s11325-025-03468-z https://doi.org/10.1007/s11325-025-03468-z

item.itunes:title: Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea-A Systematic Review
item.description:
So, what does this systematic review mean for our clinical practice?
In terms of an explicit call: watch. There is no change to our implant candidacy gate, but we must maintain a close watch on emerging trials of concurrent pharyngeal reconstruction.
Let us break down the exact decisions affected in clinic and the operating room.
First, candidate counseling. When I perform drug-induced sleep endoscopy on an Inspire candidate and observe complete oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse, I do not deny them surgery. Complete concentric collapse at the soft palate remains our only absolute anatomical exclusion. However, I change the conversation.
I tell the patient directly: if your lateral walls remained open, your expected chance of surgical success would be roughly seventy-five to eighty-five percent. With complete side-wall collapse, your expected chance of success drops by about fifteen to twenty percentage points, down to roughly fifty-eight to sixty-seven percent. But two out of three patients with this pattern still achieve success, your nightly device usage is expected to be just as high, and your stimulation voltage requirements are identical.
Second, risk stratification by body mass index. When I see complete lateral wall collapse, I look immediately at the patient's body mass index. If their body mass index is twenty-eight or twenty-nine, I am very comfortable proceeding; data from Vena and Huyett show their response rate will likely stay near seventy percent. If their body mass index is thirty-two or thirty-three, or pushing into the newly expanded thirty-five to forty range, I have a much more sobering discussion. I explain that adiposity and lateral wall collapse act synergistically to cut response rates in half, and I make weight loss and lifestyle modification an active, mandatory part of our preoperative and postoperative plan.
Third, our surgical technique. Classic U-triple-P is historical context; that is not what we do. In our practice, when we need to reconstruct the pharynx, we perform barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, or B-R-P. As you have seen me do in the operating room, B-R-P suspends and repositions the lateral pharyngeal walls anteriorly and laterally to the pterygomandibular raphe using knotless barbed sutures.

Third, our surgical technique. Classic U-triple-P is historical context; that is not what we do. In our practice, when we need to reconstruct the pharynx, we perform barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, or B-R-P. As you have seen me do in the operating room, B-R-P suspends and repositions the lateral pharyngeal walls anteriorly and laterally to the pterygomandibular raphe using knotless barbed sutures.

When you see Huyett's combination tonsillectomy data showing an eighty-five percent A-H-I reduction but a six point seven percent return to the operating room for hemorrhage, that should give you pause. Traditional cold or electrocautery tonsillectomy leaves a raw, open granulating muscle bed in an adult sleep apnea patient. If we decide to address the lateral walls surgically alongside neurostimulation, B-R-P allows us to stabilize the lateral muscular sleeve and re-approximate mucosal pillars, which provides structural lateral wall tension while mitigating the catastrophic bleeding risks of exposed muscular beds. We do not routine-order concurrent tonsillectomy on every lateral wall patient today, but in patients with prominent tonsils and complete lateral collapse, concurrent B-R-P is the technique we are watching and evaluating.

Fourth, perioperative orders. Remember our owner ruling: patients admitted for a twenty-three-hour observation stay must always be managed and documented as a twenty-three-hour observation stay. Never refer to these patients as outpatient. If we perform an Inspire implant combined with pharyngeal surgery like B-R-P in a complete lateral wall patient, they are at higher risk for airway swelling and pain. They stay on our twenty-three-hour observation pathway, receive scheduled multimodal non-opioid analgesia, and are monitored closely overnight.

Fifth, postoperative management. When these patients return at three months, remember that a titration sleep study will paint an overly optimistic picture. If a complete lateral wall patient has a borderline titration study or reports lingering daytime fatigue, we do not declare victory; we order an entire-night home sleep apnea test. And as our twenty-twenty-four data demonstrated, we maintain a very low threshold for early awake flexible endoscopy in the clinic to visualize the palate and tongue base under active stimulation and optimize our electrode programming.

Our confidence in this approach is high, supported by low-certainty GRADE prognostic evidence that clearly refutes an absolute exclusion. What evidence would move my practice to a formal change? A randomized controlled trial comparing Inspire alone versus Inspire plus barbed reposition pharyngoplasty in patients with complete lateral wall collapse, measuring entire-night efficacy and long-term durability. Until such a trial is conducted, we counsel with nuance, we stratify by body mass index, and we offer therapy to candidates who still have a two-in-three chance of success.

The formal citation for this paper is: McBrinn S, Skan O, Iacovidou A. Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnea, A Systematic Review. Diagnostics twenty-twenty-six, volume sixteen, issue sixteen, article twenty-five twenty-nine.

Before we walk into morning clinic, let me leave you with this question: when you see complete lateral wall collapse on sleep endoscopy in a patient with a body mass index of thirty-two, what is your threshold for offering hypoglossal nerve stimulation alone versus recommending concurrent palate or lateral wall surgery?

Think about that, and I will see you in the OR or clinic.

Never refer to these patients as outpatient. They stay on our twenty-three-hour observation pathway, receive scheduled multimodal non-opioid analgesia, and are monitored closely overnight.
